#6249. Dallas Wants More Gates At Love Field—And To Give Southwest Airlines A Bigger Monopoly

Dallas is opening the door to more gates at Love Field airport. Two things stand in the way. Federal law caps the airport at 20 gates, and Dallas has already negotiated a lease that would offer most of the additional gates to Southwest Airlines if the law were to change. Southwest already controls nearly all of the gates there. More room for adding Southwest flights is different than more competition for Southwest. Dallas needs a larger airport and to open itself to competition. The Dallas City Manager raised the prospect of additional gates at an aviation event last week. The airport is undergoing a $2.5 billion redevelopment that doesn’t include more gates. Former American Airlines Chairman and CEO Doug Parker defended the existing arrangement on this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. His argument rests on the existing five-party agreement, federal law and investments made in reliance on both: “agreements are agreements.” That’s only why changing the rules will be difficult, not a reason to keep limits on competition forever. Why Dallas Can’t Just Build More Love Field Gates Southwest Airlines had to fight to operate from Dallas Love Field when it first launched. It flew its first flight in 1971 after being tied up in the courts. Existing airlines agreed to leave Love Field for DFW airport. Southwest wasn’t a party to that agreement. In 1979, the Wright Amendment was passed to limit competition from Southwest Airlines. Deregulation meant that Southwest could fy beyond the state of Texas, and other carriers feared that the close-in airport they operated from would be more desirable than DFW. The upstart Southwest that fought for the right to fly was mature and pivoted to using government to its own advantage by the time they succeeded in securing the Wright Amendment Reform Act of 2006. It was a compromise among Dallas, Fort Worth, DFW Airport, American Airlines and Southwest Airlines. Southwest gained the ability to sell connecting service beyond the old geographic limits, followed by nationwide domestic nonstop service in October 2014. Love Field’s gate count had to be reduced from 32 to 20. Southwest kept most of the gates. The airport couldn’t offer nonstop international passenger service. Basically Southwest got more flying from Love Field and a monopoly there, while American Airlines got a monopoly on international service from Dallas and a cap on how much service could compete from Love Field. Initially, Southwest effectively couldn’t even fly out of Dallas – Fort Worth offering direct competition with American. The five party agreement specified that any gate Southwest operates at DFW (or another airport within 80 miles) would require giving up a Love Field gate, up to 8 total gates. That restriction ended in 2025. The provision even covered affiliates and flights carrying Southwest’s code, with exceptions for existing DFW–Midway codeshare service. Southwest couldn’t even codeshare with partners who flew to DFW, and could set up a regional affiliate to operate there. Dallas Already Gate Southwest An Option On More Love Field Gates The city council approved Southwest’s October 1, 2028 – September 30, 2040 Love Field lease covering 18 of the existing 20 gates. One gate is under Delta’s control and the final gate is under city control and can (theoretically) be used for new service. Delta Air Lines Gate At Dallas Love Field Delta Air Lines Gate At Dallas Love Field The lease anticipates what happens with a change in federal law: Southwest and the airport both agree not to oppose an increase in gates at the airport. Dallas can then seek or support the effort. If the law changes, Dallas can pursue four, eight or twelve additional gates without the usual review by major incument airlines (‘majority-in-interest’ airline review, effectively Southwest) as long as each new gate won’t cost more than $50 million in 2025 dollars. Southwest receives an option on three of four, five of eight, or eight of twelve new gates. Even after changing a law that protects incumbents, Dallas would offer most new gates to its dominant airline. Parker Explains Why American Would Fight This Parker attributed two percentage points of Delta’s margin advantage, in an internal analysis from his American tenure, to Atlanta’s lack of a competing airport like Love Field or Midway. American has a lot to lose if some Dallas travelers gain better alternatives to DFW. Parker acknowledges his bias. American has made enormous investments at DFW, and predictable rules matter when financing airports. But I’d note: The agreement is more than 20 years old. Investors who bet on government keeping out competition also take the risk that the government changes its mind. Twenty years of protection is a substantial benefit, not a guarantee of protection in perpetuity. American hsa benefited from other subsidies, too. Parker was a prime mover behind American’s receipt of $12.8 billion in pandemic payroll support, the vast majority of the second and third tranches displacing payroll the airline was going to pay anyway. American chose not to fly from Love Field. American ended service in 2009 and subleased its gates to Delta. Its later merger settlement required divestiture of the gates, but American had already stopped operating. American preferred concentrating its network at DFW but that shouldn’t give them a permanent veto over competitors serving a different airport. The Government Destroyed Gates To Make This Deal Work Parker correctly recalls the demolition of six gates at the former Legend Airlines terminal. The overall reduction was twelve gates from 32 to 20. Six of those were at the separate Lemmon Avenue facility. I covered the litigation over that terminal and its leases. The Court of Federal Claims awarded the owners $133.5 million when the city took it back through eminent domain. The Federal Circuit reversed in 2018 arguing that the fact the gates couldn’t legally be used meant it had no value. It might soon have had value. The terminal was turned into a Lincoln dealership. North Texas Has Outgrown This Bargain DFW is growing. Its new Terminal F is planned for 31 gates, all serving American, with the first 15 expected to open in 2027. Meanwhile, McKinney is preparing to launch scheduled commercial service on November 11. Different parts of the Metroplex support different airport choices. DFW, Love Field and McKinney aren’t interchangeable for a passenger near downtown Dallas. Noise and road access are real though anyone living near the airport knew there was an airport there. Additional gate construction would necessarily involve an operational, environmental and access plan. American Airlines certainly didn’t walk away from the Naples, Florida airport just because residents there don’t like commercial air service! Love Field should be allowed to grow. The additional preferential gates should be open to airlines that bring new competition, rather than committing ex ante to enlarging Southwest’s existing control. These lease commitment is an impediment to that, and actually gives American Airlines its strongest argument against expansion. Southwest built its business by fighting attempts to keep it out. American chose to leave Love Field. Neither of those things justifies keeping other competitors out of the Dallas market, or serving each of the local markets in North Texas separately. #6248. When Is An Airport Lounge Visit Not Worth It? Here’s How I Decide…

It goes without saying that a lot about the passenger experience when traveling by air has changed over the decades, both for better and worse. I think perhaps one of the most fascinating transformations we’ve seen over the years involves airport lounges, and how their purpose has completely flipped.

I’d like to talk about that in a bit more detail in this post, and share my approach to using lounges. Let me emphasize that there are of course all kinds of lounges out there, from international first class lounges, to international business class lounges, to Priority Pass, membership, and credit card lounges. This post is primarily about lounges that fall into that last category, in terms of being pretty widely accessible.

Look, I’m not trying to sound like some boomer talking about how things were in “the good old days” (nothing against boomers… hi, dad!), but I think it’s interesting to compare how things were 15-20 years ago, to how they are today.

Back in the day, airport lounges — even the most basic ones — were primarily about escaping the hustle and bustle of the terminal, and having a quiet place from which to work, with free Wi-Fi and easy access to charging ports. At the time, free Wi-Fi and charging ports in terminals were incredibly rare. The food in most standard domestic lounges sucked — it was typically cubed cheese, snack mix, and not a whole lot else.

It also goes without saying that lounges were mostly very poorly monetized. Airport real estate is incredibly expensive, and lounges were primarily a cost center for their operators, as part of an overall value proposition for travelers.

Fast forward to today, and look at the state of lounges in the United States. Lounges have much better food than they used to, and they also have much better amenities than they used to. Also, exponentially more people have access to the lounges than they used to. They’re actually pretty nice destinations in airports.

The catch is that they’ve completely lost their initial purpose — they’re no longer a place you go to escape the crowds, and quite to the contrary, they’re often the most crowded place in a terminal. In many lounges you’ll find every single seat occupied, and even a very long waitlist to get in.

Obviously this is great for monetization, since lounge operators maximize their return by having the lounges utilized as much as possible, so that the cost can be divided by the highest number of people possible. Ironically, we’ve also seen terminals largely get much nicer over the years. It’s nowadays common to see free Wi-Fi and charging ports throughout terminals, and it’s usually not too hard to just find a quiet place to sit, with more peace than you’d find in a lounge.

Back in the day, if I had lounge access, my obvious move was always to use the lounge if I had time. I mean, that seems like a pretty obvious move, right? After all, you get access to something “premium,” so you want to make the most of it. Most people with TSA PreCheck don’t say “meh, you know, I think I’ll skip that today and go through the regular line.”

At the same time, I think one has to step back and look at things objectively. At times it almost feels like people use lounges religiously in order to justify the annual fees on their credit cards, and so they can talk about how they’re eating for “free.”

You’ll often see people on social media essentially call airport lounges upper middle class airport cafeterias, and that’s probably not actually too far off in terms of how they’re practically used… and there’s nothing wrong with that!

Personally, for places with consistently crowded lounges, my approach to lounge use is pretty straightforward:

Honestly, this is one of the reasons I really love grab & go lounges, where you can pick up something to take with you. To me that’s the ideal setup, since it serves the purpose I’m actually looking for from lounges — if a lounge is going to be crowded, I’d rather just be able to grab what I’d like, and head somewhere quiet.

As someone who loves coffee, it’s why I also appreciate when lounges have great coffee to go. It’s typically the item I most want to consume at airports, and the wait for a cup of coffee at an airport can often be quite long early in the morning.

The lounge crowding issue nowadays is only made worse by the number of people who are watching videos and making calls with no headphones in lounges.

The whole concept of airport lounges has changed massively over the years. Monetization of lounges has largely gotten better, as they’ve become a key component of the credit card race that we’re seeing between airlines and card issuers.

That’s a double edged sword. On the one hand, lounges have become higher quality, on average. On the other hand, demand for them has also increased massively.

For the most part, lounges are no longer a place you go to escape the bustle of the terminal, and to use free Wi-Fi and charge your electronics. Now they’re a place you go to eat, drink, and wait in line.

The way I’ve used lounges has definitely evolved over the years, and it’s one of the reasons I appreciate the grab & go concept that we’re increasingly seeing. Unless I’m hungry or thirsty, I prefer just finding a quiet gate area.

What do you make of how airport lounges have evolved, and has your approach to using them changed?

#6247. Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

Louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”

In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the big tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

They have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.

#6245. U.S. Airlines Face New Collusion Lawsuits-Sharing Data To Keep Ticket Prices High

Airfares rose 22.4% over the past year, according to the government’s September inflation report. And American Airlines, Delta, United other major carriers are accused of using shared airfare and customer shopping data to keep ticket prices high. Two new class action lawsuits say the airlines have built a way to spot competitors’ discounts and discourage the price cutting that could save passengers money. There’s a plausible antitrust claim here. There’s also a straightforward explanation for much of the same activity: airlines need to know when they’re charging more than competitors so they can lower their prices. The kind of information sharing that’s happening does not – on its own – amount to a legal violation. I just wrote about former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker explaining how airlines use Wall Street analysts to pressure competitors to stop growing, even while denying that executives signal each other. These lawsuits raise a related question about the systems pricing departments use every day: whether airlines have agreed to share information in a way that helps them avoid competing. Cory Garner flags two new complaints: Ward v. ATPCO, filed in federal court in Seattle, and Brown v. ATPCO, filed in Virginia. Between them, they name American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, Southwest Airlines, Alaska, Hawaiian and JetBlue, along with the Airline Tariff Publishing Company and its 3Victors subsidiary. ATPCO is owned by airlines and has long distributed fares and fare rules. These cases target its newer shopping data business. Airlines increasingly generate offers that vary by channel, itinerary, bundle and customer. Those offers can be harder for competitors to observe than a published fare. Iris collects shopping data. Airlines and other participants contribute information and receive competitive information in return. PriceEye makes offers easier to compare. It supplies competitive data and alerts that draw attention to differences in pricing. DemandView identifies demand before it becomes bookings. Search activity can show where customers want to travel even when they haven’t bought tickets. 3Victors describes the information exchange as “the more you contribute, the more you receive.” And it says Iris collects all the offers returned by a shopping request, including different brands, cabins and prices which is more than an airline would get scraping a limited website search result. The lawsuits argue this gives competitors visibility into competitor pricing they wouldn’t otherwise have, including for offers that haven’t resulted in sales. An airline that might discount to fill seats instead knows rivals can quickly discover and respond to the offer, so they do not make it. If an airline expects every price cut to be matched almost immediately, it may see less opportunity to win business by cutting in the first place. The same information can make tickets cheaper. If an airline is selling a flight for $100 more than a competitor, getting an alert that they’re being underpriced lets them adjust their fares to avoid losing a sale. And better demand information can support an extra flight or a larger aircraft, adding seat supply which supports lower fares. As I’ve explained when American, United and Southwest all showed the same $523 fare, independently responding to a rival’s price isn’t an antitrust violation. Similar prices aren’t enough to establish an agreement. An airline can generally observe a publicly available price and decide to match it. Competitors agreeing to keep prices above a certain level is price fixing. An agreement to exchange sensitive information that makes competition less vigorous is somewhere in beteween – it’s alleged here that the agreement violates the Sherman Act by unreasonably restraining competition. The lawsuit itself doesn’t establish that happens – they need to get to the discovery stage and come up with something juicy. In United States v. Container Corp., the Supreme Court found reciprocal exchange of recent customer-specific prices even without an agreement to adhere to a price schedule to violate the law. On the other hand, the Court also recognized that information exchanges can improve competition. Garner points out that the old government case against ATPCO involved airlines circulating proposed fares before customers could buy them. Airlines could see whether competitors would go along with an increase before exposing themselves to losing sales. PriceEye’s ability to show current offers for future flights isn’t the same thing. A price you can buy today for travel next June isn’t advance notice of a planned price increase. I’m skeptical that what the airlines are doing here actually breaks the law. At a minimum, their defenses are pretty good. A faster, more reliable way to observe bookable fares can help airlines compete. These systems don’t make pricing decisions. There’s no common agent fixing fares. Higher fares alone don’t show this system caused them. Fuel prices and resulting capacity discipline have mattered a lot. Meanwhile, airfares have actually been falling in inflation adjusted terms and even with the recent run-up are lower than they were pre-pandemic. Assuming the cases make it through to discovery, actual contracts airlines signed and feeds will show agreements and the real data being shared, as well as how the services are marketed and discussed at the airlines. If the case goes very far, I’d imagine we’d see a settlement involving money and tighter limits on data sharing to avoid triple damages plus fees. #6244. Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

Two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artistâs back catalog with strong results on both sides. âOrigins 1971-1978â chronicles not just the Heartbreakersâ first two albums but also documents the journey that brought them there, while âThe Who By Numbers 50th Anniversary Editionâ documents the bandâs seventh album in a more traditional box set presentation. Both of the releases successfully accomplish their goals and deliver a worthwhile experience for interested listeners, but follow different paths to reach their respective sonic destinations.

âItâs not Tom Petty good.â Thatâs how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. âCould this be any band? If so, itâs not in there . . . itâs gotta be something that really adds to the canon or weâre just detracting from the canon.â

In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, âYouâre Gonna Get It!â Then thereâs âLive from the Record Plant,â originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the bandâs appearance on the BBCâs âOld Grey Whistle Test,â and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: âNo Sleep Til L.A.â and âThe Cut Out Bin.â (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.)Â

Rounding out the set is a Blu-Ray with hi-res stereo, Dolby Atmos and 5.1 immersive mixes, and importantly, a full-color 46-page âfanzineâ called âHeart Attackâ that serves as the liner notes for this box, with photographs, essays, interviews and commentary from members of the surviving Heartbreakers. There are other editions with additional advanced artifacts like posters or simulated Polaroids â my favorite is probably the âPunk to New Waveâ trading cards â but if youâre in the target market for those kinds of fun treats, youâve probably already ordered your copy.

Whatâs notable about the unreleased music featured on âNo Sleep Til L.A.â and âThe Cut Out Binâ is that it isnât just a simple compilation of demos and rough takes in a logical order of some kind, but instead is deliberately curated into the shape of an album. Itâs intended to convey the journey Petty and the band took to get to the place where theyâre going into the studio to record that first record, capturing tracks from the Mudcrutch era (Pettyâs pre-Heartbreakers band that also featured future Heartbreakers Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench) as early as 1971 and then as the Heartbreakers in their early days, learning to work in the studio in L.A. and in Tulsa, where their label Shelter Records sent them to learn how to make a record instead of running the meter on a L.A. studio.Â

The outtake record isnât trying to fabricate something that doesnât exist or inject fiction into the Heartbreakers legend, but rather, to show you how the band evolved from a bunch of kids in Florida who picked up and went out to L.A. to seek their rock ânâ roll fortunes on a wing and a prayer into a band that would end up being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Itâs expanding the legacy, not rewriting history.Â

âItâs not Tom Petty good.â Thatâs how Adria Petty, who oversees Petty Legacy, the business concern thatâs handling her late fatherâs catalog, told Salon as she described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. âCould this be any band? If so, itâs not in there . . . itâs gotta be something that really adds to the canon or weâre just detracting from the canon.âÂ

And the collection absolutely burnishes the canon. Itâs hard to listen to the selection of music and understand how any music business professional didnât think this band had serious potential. Thereâs so many standout tracks: âParade of Loons,â which opens the record, from the great rock ânâ roll tradition of writing a song from the perspective of watching the craziness unfolding around you is borderline new wave, but it also isnât â itâs easy to understand why an industry struggling to understand the new guard needed to figure out where these new guys fit, exactly â and perusing some of the photos included in âHeart Attackâ you can extend some grace on that front, because â as Adria Petty laughed, âThese are not guys you want to date your daughter, you know?â But as you learn from some of the news clips included in the booklet, Petty did not want to be co-opted into anyoneâs movement or limited by any genre.

âYouâre Gonna Learnâ is reggae-influenced at a time when that wasnât a widely known, let alone embraced, genre in American rock, and they manage to pull it off without embarrassing themselves. âUp In Mississippi Tonightâ could be an outtake from âExile on Main Street.â There are also a couple of earnest and successful Dylan homages: âWild Eyesâ and âI Canât Fight It.â If youâre going to borrow, borrow from the best (and from a guy youâre going to be on the road backing in 10 years).

Then thereâs âUnheard Kind of Hero.â This is a song that Heartbreakers keyboardist Benmont Tench had previously mentioned as a song he saw the band perform before he was in it, and how he was astounded that a band in Gainesville, Florida, was writing original material like that. In âHeart Attack,â Tench offers, âI was following Mudcrutch around because they were so good, and they played a lot of really cool covers and they played some stuff of their own,â he remembers. And when he heard âHero,â he asked a friend working for the band who sang it originally. When he was told it was an original, his reaction was, âOK, good lord. Because if you listen to that, whether he was 17 or 19 when he wrote it, the storytelling in it is the beginning.â

The box set is configured to bring the listener into the story, opening with the outtakes before taking you to the officially released albums, then live radio show and then, finally, the 1977 âOld Grey Whistle Testâ performance. But Iâd like to make the case that you should begin with the OGWT performance because it is utterly electrifying. Anglophiles are already familiar, but in case youâre not, the âOld Grey Whistle Testâ is a legendary BBC music program that was the opposite to âTop of the Popsâ in that its focus was on albums as opposed to hit singles. But this isnât an OGWT where a band plays a couple of songs; this was one of their special editions where the band gets the full show. So this is a 40-minute performance by a band that was already famous and well-liked in the U.K., a status they were still fighting to achieve back home.

Theyâre dressed in black (Benmont Tench rocking a red shirt underneath his suit jacket), Petty looking more like a gunslinger, Ray-Ban aviators and studded guitar strap, Stan Lynch singing harmony vocals over Pettyâs shoulder, Mike Campbell dropping guitar riffs and solos without breaking a sweat, Ron Blair sharing the center mic for harmony vocals but otherwise staying low-key back against the drum riser. Itâs a time machine back to 1977, with camera work more evolved than weâre used to seeing because it was a TV show about music, not a variety show that featured a band. The colors are a little over-saturated, but people who are used to watching archival rock ânâ roll clips wonât be phased. The most jarring element is whenever the camera cuts to the audience, who look like theyâd rather be anywhere else. A U.K. source shared that this was because this wasnât an audience of Tom Petty fans but rather random people whoâd put in for tickets and wouldnât have been encouraged to be enthusiastic. Petty gets his revenge, though, at the last number. (No spoilers!)

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So thereâs the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos.

âThe Who By Numbersâ was released in 1975, but this is still being declared a 50th anniversary artifact. It features 92 unreleased audio tracks, a recording of the band live in Swansea in 1976, the requisite Atmos and stereo mixes, and a video of the full concert of The Who at the Silverdome in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1975.Â

Also included is what has become a trademark for the bandâs reissue sets, a gorgeous full-color 100-page book of liner notes, interviews, lyrics, photographs and other assorted documentation. Even if you buy the CD box, youâre still getting the full-sized book because they put the CDs into an album-sized enclosure. The archivist this time is Andy Neill, one of the two names you want to see behind a Who reissue.Â

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So thereâs the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos. Townshend was approaching 30 when he began work on the songs for âBy Numbers,â and he was in the middle of a number of personal dilemmas, as well as struggling with his and the bandâs place within rock ânâ roll: âI felt detached from my own songs,â he confesses. He also rued the fact that he felt he owed his best material to the band, instead of being able to pursue more of a solo career, which all of his bandmates had done. Townshendâs âWho Came Firstâ came out in 1972, but there hadnât been anything since.

(Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) The Who, 1975

The demos are lovely, ethereal sketches, documenting Townshend breathing life into his creations for the first time. There are two demos of âKeep Me Turning,â which didnât make the cut and we wouldnât hear until it appeared on âRough Mix,â the warm and affectionate project he recorded with Ronnie Lane of the Faces two years later. A fun game is to take the Townshend demo of âSlip Kid,â where heâs kind of half-speaking, half-singing, and then compare it to Daltreyâs delivery on the finished version, which is the one song from this record that was built on the original demo. (This is a release that youâll want the good headphones for.) The highlight is probably âHow Many Friends,â which is the heartbreaker on the album; Daltreyâs read of it nails the pathos, but this version makes you wish that Pete maybe hung onto it for himself.

Up next is âTracking Sessions,â which are initial loose takes with the whole band, but not finished vocals. Itâs basically how the band taught themselves the new material, and it includes listings like âRamport Jamâ where they (sans Keith Moon, still making his way back to the U.K. after hanging out in L.A. and working on his solo record) fart around on a variety of instrumentals and a Faces song. This lasted about half an hour, but weâre getting only eight minutes; given the nature of the release, just give the fans the entire unedited mess. Throughout the sessions, you hear the band members making jokes and laughing; you hear Glyn Johns in the control room offering his thoughts; you hear Pete Townshend complaining about not being able to obtain a suitable breakfast. This stuff is gold.Â

Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between âQuadropheniaâ and âWho Are You.â

There are also lovely early run-throughs of âImagine A Manâ with a solo Townshend on acoustic and Nicky Hopkins on piano, and similarly, âThey Are All In Loveâ (a song that Daltrey did not initially want to sing) is also offered solo Pete. A prototype of âBlue Red and Grayâ is here as well, thanks to Glyn Johnsâ insistence: âI find that the hardest thing for me to do as a writer is to express optimism, general warmth and a feeling of good will to all men in a song,â Townshend said. âIt feels trite and I hate it. That song, âI Love Every Minute Of The Dayâ . . . is a prime example. Glyn Johns wanted it on the album; I cringed when he picked it. He heard it on a cassette and said, âWhatâs that?â I said, âNothing.â He said, âNo. Play it.â I said, âReally, itâs nothing. Just me playing a ukulele.â But he insisted on doing it. I said, âWhat? That fu*king thing. Hereâs me, wanting to commit suicide, and youâre going to put that thing on the recordâ.â

Disc 4 is billed âEarly Mixes & Guide Vocalsâ and is by nature more structured than the Tracking Sessions. The songs are taking shape now. Entwistle offers his approach to his âSuccess Story,â Pete sings the lead on âHowever Much I Booze,â thereâs a version of âSqueezeboxâ that the liner notes state is âaccented by tambourineâ but sounds like the cowbell on the âSNLâ âDonât Fear The Reaperâ sketch, and âDreaming From The Waistâ is a fantastic illustration of why Pete Townshend needed Roger Daltrey to sing most of his songs.Â Â

As a way to track the evolution of the song from start to finish, the inclusion of all of these different versions is an established and useful presentation device, but given their formative nature, itâs not likely that youâre going to go back to them with regularity. But thatâs not why this record exists. Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between âQuadropheniaâ and âWho Are You.âÂ

But itâs probably more accurate to state that âThe Who By Numbersâ was the record between the âTommyâ movie and âWho Are You,â which isnât a small distinction; the âTommyâ movie made the band into a larger and different flavor of rock star, one that brought in the girls because of shirtless golden god Daltrey and delivered your average punters who might not have found their way past the tunes theyâd heard on the radio. And itâs not unimportant to note that the âTommyâ movie brought the band the kind of money they hadnât yet seen.Â

Thatâs part of the cri de coeur you hear on âBy Numbers.â Itâs by no means the main thread, but it absolutely underpins Townshendâs personal anxieties. Heâs annoyed that his bandmates are off doing their own thing. Heâs perturbed that he doesnât have the time or material to make another solo record because he has to offer his best songs to The Who (and conversely, itâs kind of hilarious that he then seems panicked when he presented Daltrey with the songs heâd written for the record and ended up shocked that Rog picked âthe more personal onesâ.) NOTE: Daltrey is not responsible for the abomination that is âSqueeze Box,â that we have to blame on Ronnie Lane, who was enchanted by it.Â

The Swansea show from 1976 here isnât complete, but it is Keith Moonâs last proper show before a U.K. audience. (It was recorded with the intention of being released as a live album, and one of the original tapes went missing at some point in the 1990s, which is why the first two songs are missing.) âMy Wifeâ will sound familiar to anyone who owns the âMaximum RnBâ box set, âSqueezeboxâ is palatable because of Townshendâs giant power chords, âIâm Freeâ (introduced by Moon, who dedicates it to the occupants of the prison across the street from the venue) sounds more like the version from the âTommyâ soundtrack, and thereâs a hilarious comedic bit over âBellboy.â

But itâs the last live artifact here thatâs a truly delightful surprise. Itâs on the last disc with the Atmos remixes, and at first I feared it would be poor-quality footage added simply because it existed. But itâs far, far better than that. It is the complete show from the Pontiac Silverdome in December of 1975, cleaned up and remastered. This show set the record for the largest ever indoor rock concert attendance of 76,896, which would be broken by Led Zeppelin in the same place two years later. Because of the size of both the venue and the crowd, a large screen was set up to project closed-circuit video, a thing weâd think absolutely nothing of now, but at the time was a revolutionary development.Â

There were four cameras, and they do a more than decent job of capturing the action but donât expect any fancy camerawork or closeups of guitar solos. The sound is in mono â as the liner notes point out, âthe sound was captured via a direct line mono feed from the PA â no attempt was made to professionally record the concert for synching purposes.â Part of the âJoin Togetherâ / âRoad Runnerâ / âMy Generationâ medley ended up in âThe Kids Are Alright,â but this is the first official release of this footage.

You know what? The sound quality is more than adequate, and where it falls down the electricity coming off of that stage in this performance makes up for a multitude of sins. Roger is in Woodstock buckskin fringe, and even this primitive setup can capture that those trousers were, shall we say, form-fitting. (Wait for âMagic Bus,â which swings so much harder and better than it did later.) Daltrey introduces the âTommyâ portion by noting, âThis is how we used to do it,â and then the band proceeds to light the stage on fire. The band seems perplexed and concerned about the size of the crowd, with both Roger and Pete each taking turns to ask the crowd to take a few steps back.

This Silverdome footage is absolutely a text, and even this rudimentary capture that was meant to make sure the 76,896th guy in the back could see something is still full of electricity and life. If you were lucky enough to see the band with Keith Moon in those days, youâll remember, and if you werenât, this at least brings some of that fairy dust into your life and your house. Put it on, turn it all the way up, and enjoy it without 76,896 people stepping on your feet.

There’s now a new reason to travel to the bottom of the world.

Silversea on Thursday officially opened The Cormorant at 55 South, a new luxury hotel near the southern tip of South America designed to transform the experience of traveling to Antarctica.

Located in Chile's Patagonia region near Puerto Williams, the world's southernmost settlement, the 150-room property will serve as a luxury base and launch pad for Silversea's high-end fly-cruise trips to Antarctica — journeys that begin with a flight from Puerto Williams to a research station at Antarctica's King George Island.

Once there, travelers board a Silversea expedition ship to explore Antarctica.

Related: How to get to Antarctica: The pros and cons of flying vs. cruising

“Silversea has always been about going further, and for our guests heading to Antarctica, that journey now begins here at the southernmost hotel on Earth, with the kind of welcome they’ve come to expect from us,” Silversea president Bert Hernandez said during an unveiling event at the hotel.

TPG is one of just a handful of travel media outlets getting an early look at the property this week.

Until now, Silversea's fly-cruise passengers have stayed in non-Silversea hotels in Punta Arenas, Chile ahead of a charter flight to King George Island. The less-than-ideal arrangement meant guests were booked across various hotels, while the line was left scrambling for additional rooms whenever bad weather delayed or grounded flights to Antarctica.

Now, with The Cormorant at 55 South, guests can relax in modern luxury overnight — or sit out bad weather — just minutes from their charter flight. Better yet, the expedition begins well before they step aboard their ship.

While at the hotel, guests will be able to try on or swap their Silversea-provided Antarctica polar gear, complete biosecurity checks that are necessary before visiting the continent, and clean any personal equipment they plan to take ashore, as well as attend an initial Antarctica briefing — activities that usually take place on the ship.

Related: I just camped on the ice in Antarctica; here's how you can, too

They'll also get a chance to explore Patagonia’s breathtaking wilderness on guided excursions around the hotel, including kayaking, hiking, birdwatching and horseback riding. A shuttle bus will also take guests into Puerto Williams.

“The idea was that this wasn’t a stopover hotel. This is the first and last impression that we make on our guests, and so we wanted that to be memorable,” Hernandez said at a press conference ahead of an official ribbon-cutting ceremony.

Initially conceived in 2018 as a turnaround hub for Antarctica, the Cormorant at 55 South has become a destination that by Hernandez’s own admission is “more beautiful than anyone ever envisioned."

Designed to blend in with the environment, the low-slung hotel features soaring ceilings, concrete floors, natural wood, stone and earthy textiles punctuated by pops of orange, yellow and green — colours that echo the surrounding terrain.

Floor-to-ceiling glass means the view is never far away, be it forest, sea or snow-scratched mountains, stretching from the jagged peaks of Dientes de Navarino to the Andes in Argentina.

Related: The best Antarctica cruise vessels

“It was always incredibly important that the hotel reflect the environment,” Silversea senior vice president of expeditions Conrad Combrink said during unveiling events. Elements of fire and ice inform the design, alongside the darkness of the Drake Passage and the Beagle Channel, just beyond the hotel.

Being in the “land of fire”, the hotel fittingly has a massive indoor firepit, surrounded by lounges and easy chairs. An outside terrace offers more places to sit and take in the scenery.

Rooms are simply designed, with a view of mountain or sea, and pair a soothing mix of local wood, natural textiles and green upholstery. There’s a Nespresso machine and a small bar fridge with water and craft beer from a brewery in Punta Arenas.

Latitude 55, the onsite restaurant, showcases regional flavors, including excellent empanadas and a stand-out asado barbecue served on the first night of any stay, slow-cooked over an open fire in the hotel grounds.. At Bar Sur, guests can sample Chilean wine, enjoy a pisco sour tasting or try a cocktail made with calafete, a berry indigenous to Puerto Williams. The Uncharted Boutique is the place to stock up on beautifully made Chilean handicrafts or last-minute polar gear.

More than a hotel stay, The Cormorant at 55 South marks a wider shift for Silversea,which will now base all its Antarctica expeditions out of Puerto Williams. Previously only sailings that crossed the Drake Passage left from Puerto Williams.

While most Antarctic operators base their fleets out of Ushuaia, Argentina, Silversea is the only cruise line running operations out of Puerto Williams. Located further south along the Beagle Channel, Puerto Williams provides a shorter, more direct launch point into the Drake Passage.

Silversea's fly-cruise trips allow Antarctica-bound travelers to skip a ship-based voyage across the Drake Passage — the notoriously rough, 600-mile-wide waterway separating the tip of South America and Antarctica.

Guests fly from Santiago directly to Puerto Williams for an overnight stay at The Cormorant, before taking a charter flight across the Drake to King George Island in Antarctica's South Shetland Islands, where their expedition ship awaits. Upon return, guests spend another night at the hotel before flying back to Santiago.

Related: The ultimate guide to expedition cruising to Antarctica and beyond

The opening of the Cormorant at 55 South coincides with Silversea's largest Antarctic season to date. Fly-cruise itineraries now dominate the line’s offerings in Antarctica, accounting for 29 of its 40 total sailings across three expedition vessels: Silver Endeavour, Silver Wind, and Silver Cloud. The hotel will currently stay open from October through March, but there is talk it will open year-round, for travelers to southern Chile looking for a soft landing after adventures.

More than a place to stay,  The Cormorant makes the journey south feel like an experience in its own right — a fittingly rugged starting point for what lies ahead, plus unique bragging rights of having stayed at the southernmost hotel on earth.

#6241. U.S. Now Requires Ebola Attestation For Flights From Abroad — How To Complete It And Who Can Be Denied Boarding

Flying to the U.S. from abroad now requires an Ebola attestation. You have to confirm that you haven’t been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the previous 21 days before boarding your flight even if you’ve never been anywhere near Africa. An internal American Airlines memo explains how they’re collecting it, including what happens when a kiosk sends you to your phone and what to do if you can’t use the app. For most passengers, this is another check-in step. For someone who’s recently been to Congo, it can mean being unable to board a flight home even with a U.S. passport. Who Has To Complete An Ebola Attestation? The federal requirement took effect for flights departing for the United States at or after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 3, 2026. It applies across airlines, including foreign airlines. You provide a declaration about recent travel history. That’s it – there’s no Ebola test or vaccination certificate. U.S. citizens, foreign visitors and green card holders are covered. Passengers merely connecting through the United States are covered, too. Departures from airports with U.S. immigration preclearance still count. Domestic flights aren’t covered. U.S. territories aren’t foreign countries under this rule, so a nonstop flight from Puerto Rico to the mainland doesn’t trigger it. The form requires an attestation for each individual, including children. A parent or another authorized representative can complete it for a child or someone unable to do it themselves. The current order runs through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on December 18, 2026. The March 31, 2027 date printed on the form is the expiration of its paperwork approval, not the scheduled end of the travel requirement. How To Complete It On American Airlines American’s October 30 internal advisory lays out the airport procedures. Use the app or aa.com during check-in. The app requires you to complete the attestation before you can finish checking in. Once submitted, American adds a completion marker to your reservation. Don’t expect the kiosk to collect it. American says kiosks don’t support attestation collection. They’ll display a QR code directing you to the mobile app, and you’ll need to finish the attestation before completing kiosk check-in. No working phone? Ask for paper. American allows passengers to bring a completed paper form or request one at the airport. You can download the official fillable form here. An agent can also record a verbal attestation. You must first review the attestation wording. The agent then asks you to confirm your travel history and records that you reviewed the language and attested. Both American’s memo and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s instructions permit this. For paper, enter the name, select the appropriate option for yourself or someone you’re authorized to represent, and sign and date it. Read both pages and give the completed form to the airline. American must retain completed paper attestations for 42 days. If the app won’t let you proceed, ask an agent to check whether the attestation is recorded. American calls the completion marker ADOC. Ideally complete this before heading to the airport. If the technology fails, ask for the paper form. If You’ve Been To Congo, The Form Can Stop Your Trip The question is whether you’ve been physically present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, not whether you feel healthy or believe you were exposed. Even a connection at a Congolese airport counts, including a stop where you stayed on the aircraft. The State Department confirms that U.S. citizens are also barred from boarding commercial flights to the United States during the waiting period. Limited government exemptions exist, including authorized medical transport and limited humanitarian cases. The calendar calculation is easy to mess up: Day 0: The day you leave Congo. Days 1–21: The full calendar days you remain outside the country. Day 22: The first day you can board a flight to the United States, assuming you meet other entry requirements. Leave Congo on November 1, for instance, and the first eligible boarding date is November 23. The CDC illustrates the waiting period this way: Uganda and South Sudan have separate rules. Under the current entry restrictions, non-U.S. citizens and non-U.S. nationals, including green card holders, who’ve recently been in either country must also wait outside the United States. U.S. citizens and nationals who’ve been there, but not Congo, can return through New York JFK, Washington Dulles or Atlanta for public health screening. Airport connections count for these rules as well. How Serious Is The Ebola Outbreak? The CDC’s November 3 update, reporting data through November 1 lists 10,563 confirmed cases and 5,130 confirmed deaths almost all in Congo which is the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded. Outbreak Cases Deaths 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic About 28,600 reported About 11,300 2018–2020 Congo outbreak 3,470 reported 2,287 2026 outbreak, through November 1 10,563 confirmed 5,130 confirmed he current outbreak also passed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation; the 2018 outbreak took about 235 days. Conflict, weak health services and difficulty tracing contacts have helped it spread. Kenya and Nigeria reported imported cases in October. Ebola is extremely serious if you become infected, but the risk of becoming infected is low. The CDC reports no U.S. cases associated with this outbreak and considers introduction into the United States very unlikely. (But they aren’t always right about these things…) Ebola spreads through infected blood and other body fluids. It’s not airborne and it isn’t believed to spread by pre-symptomatic people. Taking a flight with someone exposed to Ebola isn’t going to get you sick. You need exposure to their fluids. Then illness can progress from fever, aches and fatigue to severe vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration and organ failure. The outbreak’s reported fatality rate has been around half (but probably overstates things because those dying of Ebola wind up as identified cases, while many who don’t die likely to do not). When 2021 Ebola travel restrictions were put in place, there were approved vaccines and antibody treatments. Those were for the Zaire type of Ebola while this is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which there’s no approved vaccine or specific treatment. How Much Will The Attestation Help? Ebola can take up to 21 days to cause symptoms. Someone can be infected, feel well and pass a temperature check while still incubating the disease. Waiting after leaving the outbreak country gives that infection time to become apparent before a U.S. flight. During the earlier epidemic, about 38,000 travelers received enhanced assessments at U.S. ports of entry. One was later diagnosed with Ebola who had no symptoms when he arrived and reported his illness afterward. A declaration’s effectiveness depends on truthful reporting. Requiring three weeks of extra time outside the United States creates an incentive for untruthful reporting. What To Do If You’re Restricted From Flying If you’re barred because of recent travel to an affected country, the Transportation Department’s October 28 enforcement notice preserves passenger protections: For a communicable-disease travel refusal, the passenger can choose qualifying rebooking within 90 days without penalty at the original applicable fare, or a refund for unused flights. A required significant itinerary change, such as rerouting for health screening, triggers a refund if you decline the changed trip. The separate public health travel restriction rules provide transferable credits valid for at least five years. You select the applicable refund or credit remedy, rather than collect both. If you’re refused travel on this basis, get it in writing. The airline must provide that explanation within 10 days of your request. The federal requirement took effect for flights departing for the United States at or after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 3, 2026. It applies across airlines, including foreign airlines. You provide a declaration about recent travel history. That’s it – there’s no Ebola test or vaccination certificate. U.S. citizens, foreign visitors and green card holders are covered. Passengers merely connecting through the United States are covered, too. Departures from airports with U.S. immigration preclearance still count. Domestic flights aren’t covered. U.S. territories aren’t foreign countries under this rule, so a nonstop flight from Puerto Rico to the mainland doesn’t trigger it. The form requires an attestation for each individual, including children. A parent or another authorized representative can complete it for a child or someone unable to do it themselves. The current order runs through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on December 18, 2026. The March 31, 2027 date printed on the form is the expiration of its paperwork approval, not the scheduled end of the travel requirement. #6240. Will the midterms live up to the hype? 6 key stories we’re watching

Across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans. Inflation is up, consumer confidence is down, gas and diesel prices are through the roof, largely due to the president’s war of choice in Iran. The cruelty of his MAGA agenda has roiled the country and left a bad taste even in the mouths of some of his erstwhile supporters.

Each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype. As we await the results, it’s worth taking note of several questions:

A tsunami, a trickle — or something in the middle? All are possible, but signs are pointing to significant Democratic gains, likely up to 25 seats in the House, as well as a Senate majority. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed looks increasingly likely to win in Michigan, and James Talarico has Democratic hopes up in Texas. Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska are in play, and it’s worth keeping an eye on South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana as well.

One sign will come at 6 p.m. when polls close in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, where Democrat Zach Dembo is facing off against Republican Ralph Alvarado. Once a Democratic stronghold, the seat went Republican in 2012 and, despite a close call in 2018, has remained in GOP hands since. Although the district has been gerrymandered to favor Republicans, the energy on the ground is with Dembo. If he posts and maintains a healthy lead, look for significant Democratic gains to unfold throughout the night.

What effect did redistricting have on the GOP’s chances?

The midterms will be the first test of the GOP’s redistricting strategy, which saw the party redraw congressional districts in Florida, Texas and other states, partly in response to the gains Trump made with Black and Latino voters in 2024. But polls show those margins have been largely erased as the electorate has turned on the president after nearly two tumultuous years in office, while Democratic legislatures in California and Virginia have imposed their own gerrymanders. According to a Politico poll, the GOP increasingly sees the coalition that returned Trump to office as “crumbling,” and may have gained little or nothing from all this adventurous map-drawing.

Will progressives be bolstered or chastened?

Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

The size of the blue wave could well come to be seen as a measure of progressives’ influence and power within the Democratic Party. Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins — and victories in unexpected places, such as Michigan’s 7th Congressional District where William Lawrence, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, stands a real chance of unseating incumbent Republican Tom Barrett — would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

Progressive groups are already on the offensive, getting a head start on spinning tonight’s election results, particularly in anticipation of a narrow El-Sayed win in Michigan. “Expect to hear narrow victories cited as evidence of weak electability,” a Progressive Change Campaign Committee memo obtained by Politico reads. “But a candidate’s first winning margin is not their electoral ceiling.”

Will the Haley Stevens drama matter in Michigan?

Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate primary, has brought the drama in the race’s closing days. As late as Saturday night, she pledged to colleagues and friends that she was backing El-Sayed, only to turn up hours later at a church service with his Republican opponent Mike Rogers, and endorse the former congressman in a video. The cold-dish move has virtually drowned out El-Sayed’s closing message, with Stevens being formally kicked out of the Michigan Democratic Party.

The question now is if any of it will matter, especially in light of a New York Times/Siena poll taken before Stevens’ move that showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 11 points. Michigan Republicans seem to think it won’t, telling Politico they wish the congresswoman had crossed the aisle earlier. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report agrees, moving the race in their ratings to “Leans Democratic,” a shift that was already in the works before Stevens detonated her bomb.

Still, the results in the state’s Democratic primary were far narrower than the polls showed, with El-Sayed besting Stevens by only 1%, or 14,893 votes.

The New York Times reported yesterday that the world’s first trillionaire has dropped a staggering $474 million this election cycle, an historic first. The amount has been spread out across a variety of groups, PACs and funds, but it doesn’t include the “dark-money donations” the Times reports he has also made. Most of the $168 million he contributed to the Senate Leadership Fund has served to shore up Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas, who is locked in a tight race with Talarico.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations. If the blue wave materializes, Musk can expect congressional inquiries of his activities, including his reported interventions in Russia’s war against Ukraine and his leadership of DOGE during the early months of Trump’s second administration.

Each election brings surprises. Think not one but both of Georgia’s Senate seats going to Democrats in 2020, or Republicans making big gains in New York two years later.

This is the year we could hear the echo of Georgia’s 2020 election results in another Southern state. Despite boasting large Black populations, Senate seats in South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana have long been out of reach for Democrats. But there is now a path to victory for the party’s candidates in each of those states.

In South Carolina, the GOP incumbent Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat at Donald Trump’s command following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, has proven to be a lackluster candidate, alarming even some Republicans with her performance in debates and on the stump. Democrat Annie Andrews has run a more nimble campaign, and between Graham’s performance and the national state of affairs, she appears to have narrowed the gap.

Mississippi’s incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has also run a lazy campaign, expecting to coast to victory. But the national political environment under Trump, coupled with campaign gaffes, large Black turnout in the aftermath of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and clever campaigning by Scott Colom, her Democratic opponent, have helped to put the race in play.

Louisiana is also a wild card. The state, which is one-third African American, has also seen a surge in early voting among Black residents, and according to a recent poll, the race between Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis, who is Black, is tied.

Polls are not predictive. The political history of these states continues to favor Republicans, but any of them could deliver one of 2026’s electoral surprises. If that happens, it will signal that the blue wave has become a blue tsunami.

#6238. Elon Musk is using Anakin Skywalker to cope with the midterm forecast

Move over, Haley Stevens: There’s a new competitor for the most pathetic reaction to plummeting political fortunes. Elon Musk, the former Trump administration member and the world’s richest man, has seen the midterm election forecast for conservative candidates, and he’s responded by petulantly playing with his toys.

The X owner started “Anakin-posting” on Monday. The purely online phenomenon finds far-right and MAGA nerds recasting Star Wars’ Anakin Skywalker, the man who will become Darth Vader, as a tragic hero and paragon of traditional values. A typical post uses generative AI to reframe the “Star Wars” films’ genocidal space monk as a masculine, hyper-conservative, attentive father. Musk’s post shows Anakin, as played by actor Hayden Christensen, sitting on a throne surrounded by his children, Luke and Leia, and his wife, Padme. The AI illustration has pulled liberally from all three trilogies, placing the adult faces of Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher on the children. Natalie Portman’s Padme appears to be wearing her makeup and crown from “Black Swan.” The Sith first family is surrounded by 1970s-era storm troopers and 2010s imperial guards.

“This is what they stole from us,” Musk captioned the computer-generated photo of his sci-fi fan fiction.

For the unfamiliar, Anakin was a member of an order of space knights. As a young man, he began having prophetic dreams of his wife dying in childbirth. Consumed by ambition and anger, and desperate to avoid the fate he envisioned, he was manipulated by several elderly politicians into betraying his chivalric order, killing many of his fellow knights and slaughtering an entire school full of squires for fear of retribution. Unable to save his wife, and grievously injured from a battle with his former mentor, he became a running dog of a fascist empire that aimed to rule the entire galaxy.

Right-wing young men have warped that story through the established MAGA lens of “returning to tradition,” picturing a world where having the conviction to kill a bunch of toddlers is celebrated.

The typical example of “Anakin-posting” expresses rage at a stagnant economy or lack of prospects by sharing images of Christensen’s Anakin looking stoic. MAGA influencers like Jack Posobiec have added a dash of intergalactic racism, sharing images of a young Anakin surrounded by literal aliens to hint at a pro-segregationist message. Others have reimagined Anakin’s mentors as chiding liberal scolds, grafting pink hair and a keffiyeh onto Obi-Wan Kenobi. In the pathetic galaxy of Gen Z men, anything from mid-century magazine ads to a Disney-owned sci-fi epic for children can be a stand in for their cultural grievances.

Enough time has passed between the prequels and the present that Anakin can be presented as a brooding badass. The primary criticism of the movies at the time concerned Christensen’s portrayal of Anakin as a whiny child throwing a deadly tantrum. The knotty and boring political intrigue subplots of the films have been forgotten, making it easy to gloss over Anakin being a stooge for politicians playing a game beyond his ken.

Musk, in particular, does have reasons to empathize with the “Star Wars” villain. After believing he had found a way to reshape the government toward his own ends via DOGE, he was booted when the program proved deeply unpopular. Seeing visions of a blue wave washout, he used his financial superpower to try and avoid what appears to be an oncoming loss. Separated from the levers of power and now half a billion dollars poorer, Musk has been forced to play-act a scenario where he won. His image-generating toy gave him the happy ending that politics, relationships and wealth couldn’t.

But all the AI bots can’t undo the facts of Anakin’s story. He was ultimately killed by the evil emperor he served, dying in front of the son he abandoned. His “return to tradition” was a last-minute awakening, when he was forced to confront all the harm he had done and the miserable life he had led. Now there’s something for Musk to aspire to.

The Tripadvisor-Viator experiences business has long had a "Tripadvisor" brand problem. The consolidation of their teams didn't work, and both experiences revenue and profits fell in the third quarter.

Tripadvisor is cutting jobs in its legacy hotel business as part of a new global restructuring, and CEO Matt Goldberg, whose departure the company announced Thursday, acknowledged that combining its Viator and Tripadvisor experiences teams hasn’t worked as expected.

CFO Michael Noonan is also leaving, the company said.

The consolidation of the teams in experiences, Tripadvisor’s most important segment, “hasn’t proved out as we expected, which is evident in our last 12-month performance across our points of sale,” Goldberg said.

Tripadvisor is cutting jobs in its legacy hotel metasearch business under a global restructuring, and both CEO Matt Goldberg and CFO Michael Noonan are leaving. Goldberg said the decision to combine the Viator and Tripadvisor experiences teams "hasn't proved out as we expected," a judgment backed by the numbers: third-quarter experiences revenue fell 3% and adjusted EBITDA in the segment fell 27%. Total revenue dropped 11% to $436.4 million, and the company posted a net loss of $316.9 million against net income of $48.5 million a year earlier. Goldberg said Viator and B2B2C experiences bookings grew in the low teens while the Tripadvisor channel declined by high single digits, citing SEO headwinds, weakness in the North America to Europe corridor, and execution problems. The restructuring shifts product engineering and data analytics roles into experiences and is expected to deliver $40 million in gross annualized savings. Tripadvisor said it will keep investigating strategic alternatives and will use the $685 million from the sale of TheFork to American Express to pay down debt. Goldberg leaves February 16, 2027; Noonan departs December 31, with Chief Strategy and Operations Officer Kristen Dalton stepping in as interim CFO.

#6236. New Federal Reserve Research Finds Cutting Merchant Swipe Fees Even Hurts Consumers Who Don’t Earn Rewards

You can earn no miles, no points and no cash back from your credit card and still lose if the government cuts credit card merchant swipe fees. Research from two Philadelphia Federal Reserve economists explains why: the money banks collect when you spend helps pay for better borrowing terms. That’s a problem for the retailers’ argument that consumers who don’t collect rewards are simply paying for everyone else’s vacations. I wrote this week about why the legislation threatening card rewards isn’t dead, even with Dick Durbin retiring and Roger Marshall losing his Senate seat. The political sales pitch is that reducing merchants’ payment costs saves consumers money. That isn’t true and has never been true anywhere in the world it’s been tried. It’s cover for retailers who want the benefits of accepting credit cards, but think the government should require the service be offered to them for less money. But credit cards aren’t just a convenient way to make purchases. They also provide financing for those purchases, and the merchant fee helps support that. Even A Card With No Rewards Can Give Something Back Satyajit Chatterjee and Burcu Eyigungor’s Credit Effects of Credit Card Interchange Fees uses bank supervisory data to examine an overlooked part of the debate: what interchange does to credit itself. The June 26 paper was highlighted in a new Bank of Japan summary. In the data, rewards cards have higher credit limits. Cards without rewards have lower interest rates despite higher default rates. They argue that rewards make repayment more attractive because default means losing access to future rewards. And when a bank keeps interchange instead of paying rewards, competition encourages it to offer better rates and limits to attract the customer’s business. They find that both rewards and non-rewards cardholders gain, even after accounting for higher retail prices. A bank earning money when that person buys groceries has another reason to want the account. Eliminate that revenue and the account becomes less attractive at the same borrowing terms. The adjustment could show up in the interest rate, credit limit or card approvals. Limiting interchange hurts access to credit and credit costs for the most vulnerable> Most Cards Earn Rewards—And Most Interchange Already Goes Back Out Rewards aren’t confined to a small group of people flying first class. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s latest market report says that in 2024: 80% of general purpose credit card accounts offered rewards. 92% of spending on those cards was on rewards accounts. And a separate New York Fed study finds that banks receive interchange averaging 1.82% of purchase volume and incur rewards costs averaging 1.57%. That’s about 86% of issuer interchange revenue going back out as rewards expense. Limits on credit card swipe fees actually redistribute from consumers to merchants, even as proponents seek to villify the banks. Points Aren’t The Whole Reason To Use Credit Instead Of Debit If an airline takes your money and doesn’t provide the flight, the card you used matters. So does whether a fraudulent charge has already emptied your checking account while everyone sorts out what happened. Credit cards come with federal billing dispute rights, including for purchases that weren’t delivered as agreed. With a billing error dispute, you can withhold the disputed amount during the investigation. Debit cards have fraud protections, too. But the money can already be gone from your account. Having a claim for reimbursement isn’t the same as keeping your cash available for rent while the claim gets resolved. Then there are the benefits particular cards add: purchase protection against theft or damage, extended warranties, return protection, rental-car coverage and insurance for covered travel disruptions. Interchange helps fund the card’s economics: rewards, fraud losses, dispute handling and benefits. Cutting interchange doesn’t repeal federal consumer protections athough those were imposed on an economic model that included them. And it an change what banks charge for the product, which optional benefits they offer and which customers they want. The Michigan senator wanted a âdeterrence messageâ for anyone considering working for Trump, letting them know that committing crimes or otherwise assisting in illegal or corrupt activity might result in âa ton of problemsâ for them that arenât worth the risk of legal liability. A few days after Slotkinâs warning, sources inside the White House told the Washington Sun that administration lawyers are looking at âblanket pardons for all employees involved in particular policy areas, such as deportations, war or trade.âÂ

Still, the White House is facing serious staffing issues. A September report from the Partnership for Public Service found that people Trump hires quickly leave. Not only have there been a record number of resignations, nearly half of the quitters worked less than a year for Trump.Â

On Monday, Trump himself also told the New York PostÂ that widespread pardons are on the table, not just for his staff, but for allies like Tesla CEO Elon Musk.Â Musk has good reason to be worried. Trump and his family members should also be sweating.
