He outlined how the president has made billions in office, roughly $1 million a hour, and that thereâs a great deal to learn about where that money is coming from. The Supreme Courtâs decision technically only covers crimes committed during the commission of official presidential duties. By definition, Trumpâs external money-making enterprises arenât that. His children are deeply involved in the family business as well. And as the Epstein report made sure to note, some of the crimes Trump and his associates have been accused of committing with his old friend Epstein carry no statute of limitations.

The corruption this time around is far worse than it was in Trumpâs first term, more flagrant as the air of lawlessness led to a level of carelessness that creates more prosecutable evidence. The next Democrat in office may not be like Joe Biden, who shied away from aggressive prosecution of Trump and his allies. Some of the politicians whose names are being bandied around â like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia â have been highly focused weeding out MAGA corruption.Â

Then thereâs the matter of political will. Before now, it was hard to drum up sufficient political support for accountability because voters simply didnât care enough about corruption. But as the New York Times reported last week, the issue is a rising source concern for voters. Democrats, for one thing, are doing a better job of linking Trumpâs self-dealing to the economic problems of ordinary people. For another, the Epstein scandal has broken into national consciousness, and even Republicans are struggling to sufficiently explain why Trump, despite signing a bill to release all Justice Department files related to the case, is refusing to do so.

With these winds at their back, Democrats have a much better chance of being able to conduct thorough investigations â and pursue criminal consequences for those found to have broken the law.Â

None of this week’s threats has proved real, but each one still cost a diversion, a search and a rebuilt schedule. Whoever sent them, the hoaxes have added to a list of disruptions, from conflict-driven fuel costs to closed airspace, that is making routine flying in Europe ever more challenging.

Bomb threats disrupted at least 27 flights across Europe on Thursday, the second wave this week. No explosives have been found.

French fighter jets intercepted Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome, carrying more than 150 passengers, and escorted it to the Évreux air base in Normandy. The French prime minister’s office said the pilot had not cooperated as expected, without giving more detail. Bulgaria’s air force escorted three airliners to the ground. In Madrid, Air Europa and Iberia aircraft were halted, emptied and searched after Spanish authorities received three emailed threats in less than 20 minutes, the Associated Press reported. At least 27 flights across Europe were disrupted Thursday by bomb threats, the second wave in a week, and no explosives were found in any case. French fighter jets intercepted an Aer Lingus Dublin–Rome flight carrying more than 150 passengers and escorted it to an air base in Normandy, Bulgaria's air force escorted three airliners to the ground, and Madrid authorities searched Air Europa and Iberia aircraft after receiving three emailed threats in under 20 minutes. Earlier threats on Monday and Tuesday hit flights operated by Wizz Air, Ryanair, LOT, and Scandinavian Airlines, plus a cruise ship in Greece. No government has said who is responsible, and Bloomberg reported no pattern in the carriers or routes targeted. Matthew Borie of Osprey Flight Solutions told the AP the threats could be copycats, a single person or group, or "hybrid warfare" by state actors, and pointed to a possible Russian link; Moscow has denied European accusations of sabotage this year. The operational math is the problem: each threat an airline acts on means a diversion or stopped departure, a full search, often a replacement aircraft, crews timing out, and passengers rebooked — and Skift has reported that insurance typically doesn't cover those commercial losses. The hoaxes arrive while European carriers are already absorbing jet fuel prices that have more than doubled year over year, Middle East airspace closures that lengthen Asia routes, and drone incursions at airports.

#6231. Airline Lobby Chief Says Up To 99% Of Flyers Are Happy—His Own Survey Disagrees

The head of the U.S. airline lobby says 98% to 99% of passengers are “very happy.” His own organization’s survey says 72% are satisfied (28% aren’t!) and just 31% are very satisfied. It’s good to know that most people are satisfied with flying, although the sameness of business models especially in the domestic market and variable wait times at airports, long walks through terminals, and air traffic control delays are frustrating and we’re making relatively little progress. Air travel is largely safe and affordable. Chris Sununu, the former New Hampshire governor who now leads Airlines for America, made the 99% claim on this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. He was arguing against a return to economic regulation and saying the industry needs to do a better job telling its success story. With Democrats retaking Congress, airline re-regulatoin becomes a target for Senators like Elizabeth Warren. Here’s What The Airline Lobby’s Research Found Airlines for America commissioned Ipsos to conduct its latest annual air-traveler survey. Overall in 2025: 31% were very satisfied. 41% were somewhat satisfied. 16% were neutral. 9% were somewhat dissatisfied. 3% were very dissatisfied. That’s 72% satisfied, up from 69% in the prior year (which is flat). 28% aren’t at least somewhat satisfied. Getting Someone There Isn’t The Same As Making Them Happy A passenger can reach their destination and still have spent hours dealing with flight changes, seat assignments, or cancellations and waiting in line to check bags. People are more happy when flights operate on-time. They’re happier when the middle seat next to them is empty. They’re happy when the employees they interact with seem not to hate their jobs. Airlines are now trying to get passengers to spend more for their product, move their loyalty and put the airline’s credit card at the top of their wallet. Delivering on-time transportation is baseline – necessary, but not sufficient. The Industry Has A Better Argument Available Sununu is right to reject a return to government deciding which airlines can fly which routes and what they can charge. Customer complaints aren’t a reason to restore that system. We need competition, fewer barriers to entry into the industry for new carriers and more innovative business models and aircraft. The airline industry has been subsidized, and it’s largely sclerotic. More regulation would make that worse – but simply denying that air travel could be better – that ‘99%’ of consumers are happy – isn’t the right case to be making. #6230. “It’s them, not me”: Trump rages at Fox News over election coverage

President Donald Trump fumed at Fox News on Election Day, accusing the conservative network of turning against him, giving Democrats too much airtime and driving away its own viewers.

“FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me.”

﻿

Trump insisted his own popularity remained strong, claiming his numbers were “better than they have ever been” and citing a CNN poll that he said showed overwhelming Republican support for him.

The president also accused Fox News of deliberately undermining him through its polling.

“The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask,” Trump wrote. “Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLS***!'”

His grievances extended beyond the network’s programming. Trump questioned why Fox Corp. was financially supporting Democratic politicians and organizations, naming House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Reps. Jamie Raskin, Ted Lieu and Pete Aguilar, along with several Democratic campaign committees. He did not provide figures to substantiate his allegations.

Trump also singled out Jessica Tarlov, the Democratic strategist and co-host of Fox News’ “The Five,” with a personal insult while watching the network’s election coverage, a complaint he brought up in previous posts.

“I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me,” Trump wrote, adding that he would change channels until she was off the air.

Fox News has experienced a ratings decline, although Trump’s explanation for the drop is unsubstantiated. Nielsen data showed the network’s total-day audience fell 27% in October compared with the previous year, according to TheWrap. Fox nevertheless remained the most-watched cable news network.

Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch attributed the decline to viewer fatigue during an earnings call Monday.

Trump, however, insisted the network’s coverage of him was responsible.

“They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!” he wrote. “This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”

#6228. Jon Ossoff projected to handily win reelection in Georgia

Sen. Jon Ossoff easily defeated a challenge from Republican Rep. Mike Collins to hold on to his Georgia Senate seat on Tuesday, according to AP projections.

After Donald Trump carried the state in 2024, early forecasts predicted tough sledding for Ossoff. But during a brutal government shutdown — the longest on record — the senator signaled he was willing to stake his candidacy on protecting Affordable Care Act subsidies, and he proved an adept campaigner who was hyper-focused on Georgia issues. Ossoff focused his stump speeches around affordability, skyrocketing inflation and foreign entanglements, hammering Trump for his costly war with Iran.

For his part, Collins’ candidacy was hamstrung by controversies involving his payroll and affiliation with alleged white nationalists.

Frequently floated as a 2028 contender, Ossoff adopted a fighter’s stance at his campaign events. Like feisty Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, the senator took every opportunity to land a jab against Republicans, occasionally causing some monocle-popping among centrist commentators still holding on to the idea of the dignity of the presidential office. In August, he drew jeers and applause for making light of the rumors surrounding Trump aide Natalie Harp.

“So [Trump] doesn’t want to do this job,” Ossoff said . “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Ossoff, for his part, has said he has “zero interest in running for president.” His victory speech, which will come later tonight, will be studied by pundits seeking to divine his intentions.

#6225. I Went Dumpster Diving At Wendy’s And Bought $100,000 In Stickers—All For Airline Miles

I found her video via Mommy Points and genuinely laughed pretty hard, probably because it hits a bit close to home.

Every ridiculous instruction comes with absolute confidence. Don’t have a pet? Doesn’t matter. Buying all that dog food sounds expensive? It’s going to pay for itself. You’re confused? Just keep following the steps. We’ve got circles and arrows for you.

Watch Britt Migs explain “how those credit card point people sound.”

One commenter explains, “This doesn’t work if you already had a SwizzyPay account.” Someone else offers a real service to help people book lie flat seats, prompting Britt to reply, “omg i’ve summoned one of.”

That’s us. Someone says the process sounds exhausting and our instinct is to explain one more exception, certain that this will clear everything up.

The closest real example might be my strategy for the 2011 US Airways Grand Slam promotion. You earned a big bonus by completing transactions with different partners. Getting to 36 qualifying activities earned 100,000 bonus miles.

Transferred points from five different hotel programs. Converted four American Airlines miles into one US Airways mile. Spent 500 miles on a magazine subscription I didn’t want. Installed the airline’s browser toolbar, performed three searches to earn one mile, and then disabled the toolbar.

This isn’t even something from a less mature period of my life. Less than two weeks ago, I explained how I redirected my wife’s Bilt authorized-user rewards after using up my five points accelerators. Her points go to her account. Her separate Bilt Cash goes to her account, too. That lets her use her own accelerators and separate transfer bonus allowance. Then each to have a primary card and an authorized-user card on the other’s account to take advantage of double transfer bonuses.

The old deals had names like BigCrumbs, OneVanilla, and Bluebird. SwizzyPay (formerly Buck Buck) fits right in. Did you know that GooglePay used to be known as ISIS until the Islamic State ruined that brand? BigCrumbs, OneVanilla, and Bluebird. In 2014, I explained a chain involving buying American Express gift cards through a cash back portal, using those to buy OneVanilla Visa cards at CVS, loading the Visa balances onto Bluebird at Walmart, and moving the money back to a bank account. You needed stores that would cooperate. The cash back helped cover the fees. Walmart was too far away for the economics to work for me but I had alternatives! Christmas morning, buying six figures in stickers. In 2009, combining a US Airways shopping bonus with Track-It-Back’s earning rate produced 140 miles per dollar. But first you needed purchases from 5 total merchants to qualify (but not more than 10!). I arranged over $100,000 in sticker purchases across accounts belonging to friends and colleagues, generating over 16 million miles. This involved little purchases like $2 tree donations and $5 gift cards before the big orders. The product helped recover lost belongings. A charitable donation reduced the tax basis. I had no other use for the product. Handwrite 94 cards and send them to Kalamazoo. IHG’s 2015 promotion offered at least 500 points per mailed sweepstakes entry. Ninety-four separate entries meant at least 47,000 points. A reader offered to do all the handwriting and mailing for $136. I used the service. We had created an industry to spare people the manual labor of telling a hotel company their address 94 times. Buy money, deposit money, use the money to pay for the money. The U.S. Mint sold dollar coins at face value, accepted credit cards, and shipped them free. People earned rewards, deposited the coins, and paid their card bills. The federal government wanted coins circulating. We wanted miles. The boxes were heavy. Become important to a casino because another casino thinks you’re important. Nick Reyes documented the Wyndham-to-Caesars-to-Hard-Rock-to-Ocean chain: start with hotel status from a credit card, match it through casino programs, make the required visits to Atlantic City, and end up with an MSC cruise offer. There were still costs, including gratuities. The card-based Wyndham entry route ended in 2025. But for a time, explaining how your credit card bought you a cruise required a detour through New Jersey. MilesTalk literally trademarked ‘status match merry-go-round’. Fly around the world so you can afford to fly around the world. The 2024 SAS challenge offered a million points for flying 15 different eligible airlines. My advice included looking for short Virgin Atlantic flights in the Caribbean and KLM flights within Asia to check off carriers more efficiently. A normal person might have stopped at “15 different airlines.” Then there’s David Phillips buying 12,150 pudding cups and arranging for food banks to help remove the barcodes. Britt’s 100 bags of dog food barely qualify as a starter purchase. As for me, I’ve gone dumpster diving for Wendy’s soda cups and attended a hair loss consultation with a full head of hair. The cups earned AirTran flights. The consultation earned Delta miles. Credit: runner1928 via Wikimedia Commons What Kind Of Person Finds This Fun? The points obsessive enjoys systems, notices exceptions, and hates leaving value on the table. There’s real satisfaction in understanding something complicated and making it work. The business class seat is valuable. Knowing how you got it is part of the thrill. So is explaining it afterward. Incessantly. To anyone who will (barely) listen. The hobby even calls a spouse “Player Two.” A person you promised to love for the rest of your life has become a tool for scaling. One commenter on Britt’s video wrote: We used to know what plants were edible. So glad my brain is focused on knowing credit card point schemes instead. Modernity is awesome The appeal is that reading the rules can actually change the outcome. Most customers accept the price. We want to find the exception, prove it works, and tell someone about it. It’s also a remarkable use of human effort. Shipping coins around the country and handwriting the same information 94 times can be profitable. And the person congratulating himself on outsmarting marketing may spend more time thinking about a bank’s products than the bank’s own employees. The financial mistake is counting every benefit at full retail while forgetting the costs. A $12,000 business class ticket doesn’t mean you saved $12,000 if you’d never have bought it. Annual fees, purchases you wouldn’t otherwise make, forgone cash back, and an inconvenient itinerary are costs. But the opposite mistake is pretending every spare hour could have been sold at your professional billing rate. Some people enjoy crossword puzzles or football. Some enjoy figuring out which airline program will book another airline’s seat for fewer points. The rewards can be extraordinary. In 2002, I wrote about buying 21 magazine subscriptions for $1,258.95, earning Starwood points, transferring those to Qantas with bonuses and a favorable conversion ratio, and getting enough miles for a roundtrip on British Airways Concorde. So I laughed at Britt’s video. I also noticed she never tells us which program the 100,000 points are in. Before I buy the dog food, I’m going to need to see the award chart. #6223. Keisha Lance Bottoms set to become first Black woman governor in US

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

The contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

Nights and seats booked, which include homes, hotels, experiences and services, grew 16%. Airbnb didn’t point to a single factor.

Airbnb said third-quarter revenue grew 19% to $4.9 billion, its fastest growth in more than three years and ahead of both Expedia Group, which grew 12%, and Booking Holdings, whose revenue fell 1% after a $1 billion accounting charge tied to a possible FTC settlement. Nights and seats booked — a combined measure covering homes, hotels, experiences, and services — rose 16%, against 7% room night growth at each of its two larger rivals, though the metrics are not directly comparable. Airbnb attributed the acceleration to demand across all regions and to product work including search and merchandising, pricing tools, flexible payments, and Reserve Now, Pay Later, which it said has extended booking lead times. The expansion beyond homes is showing early traction: Airbnb now lists thousands of independent and boutique hotels in 60 top destinations, up from 20 in May, and said about 35% of guests whose first booking is a hotel come back to book a home. Car rentals, sourced from Expedia's CarTrawler, have become one of its most popular services. AI customer support now runs in 50 languages, resolved roughly 40% of all support issues without a human agent, and cut support costs per booking 17%. Net income rose 35% to $1.9 billion, and Airbnb raised full-year revenue guidance to 16-18% growth from a prior "mid-teens" forecast.

#6221. Andrews defeats Graham in South Carolina Senate shocker

Dr. Annie Andrews will be the first Democratic senator from South Carolina since 1998, according to AP projections. In a stunning upset, she defeated the incumbent Republican Darline Graham, who was hand-picked by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, following his death in July.

A pediatrician, Andrews positioned herself as an antidote to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA agenda. Her campaign launch video hinged on measles outbreaks and the harm of anti-vax sentiments at the highest levels of public health. She described Kennedy as the “brain worm guy” and slammed Trump’s Cabinet as uniquely unsuited to their positions.

The race was never supposed to be close. South Carolina is about as red as you can imagine. The haven of cheap gas and fireworks hasn’t elected any Democrat to statewide office since 2006. Trump carried the state by 17 points in 2024.

Unlike her sibling, who shifted from staunch Trump critic to late-in-life ally, Graham was joined at the hip to the Trump administration from the outset. The president’s high disapproval ratings worked to turn the typical GOP lay-up into a closely contested race.

But Graham, a novice politician, did herself no favors. She flubbed softball questions around foreign affairs on the debate stage, a strong suit of her hawkish brother. Her dismal poll numbers pushed Trump to rally for Graham repeatedly in the state, cementing even stronger associations between the Republican nominee and Trump’s unpopular policies.

High early turnout among Black voters in the state also spelled trouble for Graham. The community, which is largely Democratic, turned out in high relative numbers and helped swing the race toward Andrews.

The Democratic candidate worked to avoid the associations with national party leaders that hamstrung Graham, refraining from appearances with prominent Democrats in the race’s final weeks. Andrews painted herself as a pragmatist, willing to work with national Republicans to score wins for South Carolinians. Late last month, Andrews received a shocking bipartisan endorsement from two former governors of South Carolina. Republican David Beasley joined Democrat Jim Hodges to support Andrews over Trump-backed Graham, saying Andrews was the only candidate focused on “making things better.”

Planning and taking a trip can be exciting, but unexpected events can disrupt even the most meticulously organized vacations. Sudden illness, severe weather and unforeseen circumstances can throw a wrench in the works, forcing you to change your plans and seek compensation.

Fortunately, many credit cards include trip cancellation and interruption insurance at no additional cost when you use your card to book travel. The right card can reimburse nonrefundable expenses if your plans fall apart.

Here are the best credit cards for trip cancellation and interruption insurance — and how their coverage compares.

The cards listed above offer some of the strongest trip cancellation and interruption protections available. However, many other travel credit cards also include some form of coverage — often with lower limits.

Related: Credit cards with travel insurance

Trip cancellation and trip interruption insurance can reimburse prepaid, nonrefundable travel expenses if you cancel or alter your trip for a covered reason. Coverage limits, eligible expenses and qualifying events vary by card.

In general, trip cancellation insurance applies when you must cancel before departure, and trip interruption insurance applies if your trip is cut short after it begins.

Unlike travel insurance policies with optional “cancel for any reason” coverage, credit card coverage typically applies only to specific covered events outlined in your card’s guide to benefits. Covered reasons often include illness, injury or severe weather, but exclusions apply.

Because benefits can change, always review your card’s guide before booking travel.

Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection?

Chase credit cards offer some of the most comprehensive trip cancellation and interruption protections among major issuers.

The and the each provide coverage of up to $10,000 per covered person and $20,000 per trip. Despite their different annual fees, $95 and $795, respectively, both cards offer top-tier protection limits.

The , United's highest-tier personal card and the one best suited for frequent United travelers, also provides coverage of up to $10,000 per covered person and $20,000 per trip, per the card's Guide to Benefits.

You and your immediate family members may be eligible for coverage when you pay for all or a portion of your trip with an eligible Chase card or redeem rewards associated with that account, including through Chase Travel℠.

Other Chase cards offer lower limits. For example, the (see rates and fees), the (see rates and fees) and the (see rates and fees) typically provide coverage of up to $5,000 per covered person and $10,000 per trip.

Meanwhile, cards such as the (see rates and fees), the (see rates and fees) and the (see rates and fees) also offer trip cancellation and interruption insurance but with lower coverage limits. These cards typically reimburse only nonrefundable common carrier fares and offer significantly smaller per-person caps than the Sapphire cards.

Coverage generally applies only to the portion of the trip charged to your eligible card (or booked using associated rewards).

For example, if you pay for a nonrefundable hotel stay with gift cards but charge your flight to your Chase card, you likely won’t be reimbursed for the hotel if you cancel — even if the flight was covered.

Always consult your card’s guide to benefits for full terms, conditions and exclusions.

Related: Your guide to Chase’s trip insurance coverage

Select American Express cards offer trip cancellation and trip interruption insurance. Each benefit provides coverage of up to $10,000 per covered trip, with a separate maximum of $20,000 per eligible card per 12 consecutive months.

*Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Unlike many issuers, eligible American Express cards may also cover traveling companions, not just immediate family members. A traveling companion is defined as someone who has made advance arrangements to travel with you or your family members for all or part of a covered trip.

To qualify, you must charge the full cost of round-trip common carrier transportation to an eligible Amex card or use a combination of your card and Membership Rewards points, vouchers or loyalty program certificates.

You can find benefit guides for eligible cards on Amex’s website.

Related: Your complete guide to travel protections on American Express cards

Who is covered by credit card trip cancellation and interruption insurance varies greatly. For example, eligible premium Chase cards cover the cardholder and immediate family members when the cardholder pays for all or a portion of a trip with their card account or rewards associated with their account.

On the other hand, eligible American Express cards cover the cardholder, their family members and traveling companions. The guide to benefits for eligible Amex cards defines a traveling companion as “an individual who has made advanced arrangements with you or your Family Members to travel together for all or part of a Covered Trip.”

Definitions of “family member” and “traveling companion” differ, and benefits are subject to change. Review your guide to benefits to confirm eligibility before booking.

Related: Are authorized users covered by Chase’s credit card travel insurance?

A benefits administrator can usually walk you through specific steps to make your claim. Luckily, many card issuers also allow you to make claims online, so you may not even need to hop on the phone to send any physical documents.

Related: Who is covered by credit card travel insurance?

Generally, trip cancellation and trip interruption insurance will cover nonrefundable expenses if you need to cancel your trip (or the remainder of your trip) due to a natural disaster. However, credit card insurance policies vary, so check your benefits guide for specific exclusions.

Note that you must book your trip before the natural disaster starts to be covered. If a storm or hurricane is named and you book your trip afterward, you likely won’t be covered.

Related: 4 times your credit card’s travel insurance can help with travel woes, and 7 times it won’t

Trip cancellation and interruption insurance can be one of the most valuable — and overlooked — benefits on a travel credit card.

Coverage details vary widely by issuer and by card, so it’s important to review your guide to benefits before booking.

For expensive trips, you may still consider stand-alone travel insurance, but the right credit card can provide meaningful protection without paying extra.

#6217. Talarico, Hinojosa win big in Texas despite Elon Musk’s millions

James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

This marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

The big blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a new record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

Although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

Although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.

Qatar’s visitor numbers are recovering on road traffic across the Saudi border, while air arrivals keep falling. Drive-in visitors tend to make shorter trips, which limits how much they can do for hotels.

Qatar’s tourism recovery from the U.S.-Iran war is running on road traffic across the Saudi border, a Skift analysis of Qatar Tourism data shows. .

International visitor arrivals in October totaled 336,000, down 10% from the same time last year, according to Qatar Tourism’s monthly arrivals data. September’s arrivals were up 1%. Both are a sharp turnaround from March, when arrivals fell 82% year over year to 63,000.

Qatar received 2.95 million visitors in the first 10 months of 2026, down 24% from 3.9 million in the same period last year.

Road is the only part of Qatar’s arrivals that is growing. Land arrivals, which all come through Qatar’s sole land border with Saudi Arabia, rose 18% year over year in October. Air arrivals fell 19%, registering an eighth straight month of decline.

Qatar's tourism recovery from the U.S.-Iran war is being carried by road traffic from Saudi Arabia, a Skift analysis of Qatar Tourism data shows. International arrivals reached 336,000 in October, down 10% year over year, and 2.95 million in the first 10 months of 2026, down 24% from 3.9 million a year earlier. Land arrivals through Qatar's only land border rose 18% in October and now make up 31% of all arrivals, up from 24% a year earlier. Air arrivals fell 19%, an eighth straight monthly decline, after collapsing 90% in March. Shaza Doha general manager Siddhartha Chowdhry said several pre-war source markets have yet to return, citing travel advisories, reduced airline seat capacity, higher travel insurance costs, and weaker traveler confidence. Hotel occupancy in September was 61.5%, down three percentage points year over year but well above April's 44.5% low, with RevPAR down 4%. Sea arrivals have been near zero since March, and the new cruise season is a test of whether ships return. Qatar is again leaning on events — MotoGP in early November and F1 from November 27 to 29 — after last year's F1 weekend drove ADR of about $241 and roughly 92% occupancy on its opening Friday. ValuStrat's Saad Lodhi expects cooler weather and F1 to lift performance but warned against counting on a repeat of last year's peaks.

This was a historic smackdown, a massive, crushing defeat on a scale suffered by no incumbent president in living memory. Greg Abbott â who lost his seat to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in one of Tuesday nightâs numerous shockers â of being a RINO sellout. Then again, in an ass-backward way, Trump has a point. He didnât do this all by himself; no one could have managed that. He loaded up the pipe with bigotry and xenophobia and fear and insane conspiracy theories, and adult Republican humans who used to believe in wrong-headed but somewhat sane political doctrines inhaled it all eagerly, persuading themselves that the resulting high would insulate them from the failure of their ideas. The president corrupted and enslaved a historic American political party with a complicated but illustrious history, the party of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant and Dwight Eisenhower and Ronald Reagan. Iâm not the biggest fan of that party either, but it has certainly had its moments, including the first woman to serve in both houses of Congress and the first Black man elected to the U.S. Senate. Trump insisted that it surrender everything to him â its principles, its history and its soul, if political parties have such a thing â and as in every fable about making a deal with the devil, now it has been destroyed.

#6203. Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

This article was originally published on The Conversation.

Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later said, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as âreduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.â

The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like âspontaneous morning erectionsâ as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administrationâs tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call âcringe fascism.â

For some time thereâs been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trumpâs presidency could be considered âfascist.â Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

And thatâs where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,âcringeâ is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesnât seem to be to them.

For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing â or cringe.

But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegsethâs testosterone policy, hides a much more serious â and to some critics, fascist â reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

As Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trumpâs authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. Thatâs especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trumpâs inner circle.

Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of âblood and soilâ in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to âDefend the Homeland.â

And then there are the attacks on the press as the âenemy of the people,â echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trumpâs banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoevenâs âStarship Troopers,â in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid âcringe.â

Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

On the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on menâs bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Hustedâs rear feels deeply surreal.

Trumpâs seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

It is difficult to see criticsâ view of Trumpâs second term as âfascistâ when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trumpâs supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that â as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia shows â regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet thatâs why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

Matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison

#6201. The petty joy of a blue election night

Ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”

Shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

So we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

“If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

“You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

Election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

Neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue showed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

“What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”

And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

Peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

Most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Big Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood.  On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his new network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

But Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

Still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”

Once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

This is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he said.

So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

It was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. New Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

Once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she said, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”

So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory said, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”

That moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he said. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”

But by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

As great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that big tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Rooseveltâs long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the New Deal agenda.Â

Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently itâs always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginiaâs Joe Manchin and Arizonaâs Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.Â

In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives âoverreading the mandate,â the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this issue there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll showed that 90% of voters said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say thatâs a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.Â

Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

#6188. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

In South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

Democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

With GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

Among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

#6182. One industry faces multitrillion-dollar reckoning after historic midterm election reshuffle

Alpha Compute CEO Brittany Kaiser argues that common-sense regulations, not sweeping bans or moratoriums, are the key to unlocking economic growth while protecting local communities.

President Donald Trump has thrown the federal government's weight behind massive data center build-outs needed to power the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom. But a historic Democratic sweep in Texas has put one of the nation's biggest AI infrastructure hubs under new political leadership, raising questions about the future of billions of dollars in planned investments.

The victories marked a historic midterm night for Texas Democrats, who captured the governor's mansion for the first time in more than three decades and won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1988.

Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. data center power capacity through 2030. With at least 248 projects planned across the state, investment bank Jefferies estimates that 13.3 gigawatts of announced developments could be at risk under a moratorium backed by Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa.

ONE STATE IS GROUND ZERO AS TRUMP'S MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR TECH AMBITIONS FACE A MIDTERM TEST

Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. capacity through 2030. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Texas was hardly alone in facing growing opposition to data center development. In Ohio, voters weighed 21 data center-related ballot questions across 18 communities in the midterm elections, more than any other state, highlighting the mounting resistance to America's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure.

The results this week are now forcing some developers to reconsider where to invest billions of dollars in future projects as political power shifts.

"It makes us and our investors pause and think if we should be investing somewhere else," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital following the Republican bloodbath in Tuesday's election.

Kaiser warned that political shifts in traditionally Republican states could push billions of dollars in planned investments elsewhere, including overseas, as companies weigh growing opposition to data center development — especially within the Democratic Party.

"There's new decision making that needs to come into play and a lot more to think about than there was before the election," she said.

IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW

A data center stores and processes the digital information that powers services people use every day. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)

But relocating projects already underway is far more complicated, particularly when developers have secured land, negotiated power agreements and committed substantial capital.

"It's not very easy to pivot after you've already made contractual and financial commitments to these types of builds," Kaiser said.

For projects still in the pipeline, however, companies have more flexibility. Kaiser said Alpha Compute has already invested in data centers in Canada, Europe and Mexico, where regulatory approvals are more straightforward.

The backlash highlights growing tensions between Washington's push to accelerate AI development and voters' concerns about electricity costs and the impact of data centers on their communities.

Kaiser urged incoming lawmakers to strike a balance between addressing community concerns and preserving what she called "the biggest economic opportunity of our generation."

The AI boom is accelerating demand for data centers across Texas as companies seek more space, power and infrastructure to support increasingly intensive computing needs. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

"It's really important, yes, to make sure that data center companies are good actors and are doing things the right way," she said, calling for "common sense legislation and regulation" that allows developers to work with lawmakers and local communities.

"If we can abide by those rules, then bans and moratoriums should not be the answer," Kaiser said. "It's just let's sensibly regulate and move forward in a way that is positively impactful for communities."

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

#6179. Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

For all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world â and there are so, so many â heâs also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal governmentâs medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if weâre not careful, weâre all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, âKlara and the Sun.â After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the filmâs distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movieâs wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedyâs reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

Waititiâs childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isnât akin to Donald Trumpâs most damning sins, Waititiâs mockery is a symptom of a problem that wonât be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that âKlara and the Sunâ was âreboundingâ with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the filmâs 25% critics score. (For what itâs worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a filmâs quality.) âI havenât read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,â Waititi captioned the post. âBut I do listen to the people . . . Letâs spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldnât achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.â

Reading Waititiâs emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trumpâs favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a âSAD!â at the end of Waititiâs caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trumpâs poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, âThe critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.â)

Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititiâs caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trumpâs agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesdayâs midterms. But judging by the results, MAGAâs influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended â at least for now.

Not to be all, âOh, wonât someone think of the celebrities?â about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that itâs bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isnât akin to Trumpâs most damning sins, Waititiâs mockery is a symptom of a problem that wonât be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, âJojo Rabbit,â which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propagandaâs influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititiâs writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: Itâs downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics â people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi â just six years later.

But this is the rot that social media creates. Whether itâs Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.Â

For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the monthâs salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today â to pursue oneâs passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one â is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesnât stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a new project after a string of flops.

If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, itâs that things arenât just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

What Waititi fails to realize is that heâs not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But thatâs hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social mediaâs effect on human behavior, itâs had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyoneâs a critic, then no one is, and thatâs precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like theyâre poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

But itâs not just Waititi whoâs vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether itâs a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer techâs sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. Iâve seen this affect criticsâ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

Whatâs most concerning in Waititiâs response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before itâs even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other peopleâs perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion shows maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger wonât do anything for a personâs growth, artistic or otherwise. Americaâs politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

If Americaâs blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerbergâs Instagram, we owe some props to one of the centuryâs most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkinâs âThe Social Reckoningâ actually got a few things right. In last monthâs companion piece to âThe Social Network,â Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his directorâs eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. âIâm worried that the parts of directing that Iâm not good at are those parts you canât learn,â he admitted.

While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkinâs introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, itâs that things arenât just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.
